To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) carotenoid pigmentation is a function of carotenoid accumulation in the tissues, and (2) the carotenoid accumulation patterns are consistent with different priorities for carotenoids in males and females.

1) the same set of dietary and metabolic carotenoids was found in the plasma, liver and adipose tissues of male and female birds, and 2) the same set was found in beaks of male and female finches, but males had more of them than did females.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the allocation of carotenoids in the tissues of zebra finches, a species in which both sexes have colorful beaks and males also have colorful legs.
the allocation of carotenoids to different tissues and the implications of such allocation strategies for the acquisition and maintenance of sexually selected traits.
the distribution of carotenoids among the tissues of zebra finches and the factors that influence the distribution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the allocation of carotenoids in zebra finches follows the same pattern as in other species: males allocate carotenoids to coloration and females allocate carotenoids for reproduction.
males are “color specialists,” while females are “nutritional specialists” with regard to carotenoid allocation.

the allocation of carotenoids in this species is consistent with the different life‐history priorities of the sexes, and that the different priorities of males and females are manifested in their different tissue distributions of carotenoids, and that this pattern of sex‐specific allocation is consistent with the hypothesis that the different carotenoid profiles of the sexes are due to different priorities of carotenoid allocation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the carotenoid‐rich integumentary tissues of birds, such as beak, legs, and feathers, are the result of a dynamic interplay between carotenoid acquisition from the diet, carotenoid metabolism, and carotenoid allocation among body tissues.

carotenoid pigmentation in zebra finches is determined by the relative amounts of dietary and metabolically produced carotenoids in circulation, liver, and fat stores, as well as the presence of specific carotenoid derivatives (e.g., red ketocarotene‐oxides) in the beak and, for males only, the legs, and that these patterns of allocation reflect different priorities of males and females for carotenoids.

males have higher carotenoid levels in circulation and in the retina and females have higher levels in the liver and adipose tissues, and that these patterns are consistent with males' and females' different life‐history priorities.
The main takeaway from our work is that

carotenoids are not just important for integumentary coloration, they are also important for many other physiological functions in the body, and the allocation of carotenoids to these various functions may vary between the sexes.
